sections.h2: What is Hancock County, Kentucky like for someone selling a house?
sections.html:
Hancock County hugs the Ohio River on Kentucky's northwest side. Hawesville is the seat, Lewisport is the biggest town, and the river separates the county from Spencer and Perry counties in Indiana. The county was carved out in 1829 from slices of Breckinridge, Daviess and Ohio counties and carries the name of John Hancock. Its courthouse dates to 1868 and was renovated in 1978, and the county sits inside the Owensboro metro area.

Industry lines the riverbank. The county industrial foundation describes three aluminum plants and a paper mill, with over 2,000 workers between them, plus smaller manufacturers. Hawesville's 1902 railroad depot, where Harry Truman stopped during his 1948 campaign, is now the county museum and opens on Sundays from April through October. Vastwood Park covers nearly 400 acres on US 60 between Hawesville and Lewisport, with a 19 acre lake and a paved 1.1 mile trail.

The Census Bureau counted 15 building permits for 2025. A Hancock County seller is usually offering a resale house in a small market, where new construction rarely sets the price.

sections.h2: Which offices handle a Hancock County property tax bill?
sections.html:
Three offices share the Hancock County Administration Building at 225 Main Cross Street in Hawesville, and each has a separate job.

  • Sheriff, first floor: takes payment. Phone 270-927-6247, mail to P.O. Box 427. The posted hours are 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. on weekdays.
  • PVA: values property, and has no say over rates or payments. It reads the market each January 1 and aims for what a willing buyer would pay. Phone 270-927-6846, mail to P.O. Box 523.
  • County Clerk, second floor: keeps land records and processes delinquent real estate taxes. Phone 270-927-6117, mail to P.O. Box 146.

The state's Department of Revenue supervises the PVA's work and runs yearly studies in every county to check that assessments meet constitutional standards.

sections.h2: When do Hancock County tax bills fall due?
sections.html:
Bills reach the sheriff by mid September. Until then the PVA mails the current year bill to whatever in care of address appears in the deed. KRS 134.015 gives a 2 percent discount for full payment on or before November 1 and sets face value for the rest of the year.

Miss that and January adds 5 percent. Past January 31 the penalty doubles to 10 percent and the sheriff tacks on another 10 percent, which the state describes as 21 percent combined. When the state delays mailing, an alternative schedule gives 30 days per stage instead. The bill in your hand carries the dates that apply.

Whoever owned the house on January 1 is the taxpayer of record for that year, so a closing in October or November is the moment to ask the sheriff for the exact discount cutoff.

About 20.6 percent of residents are past their 65th birthday, so a good share of Hancock County owners are old enough for the homestead exemption described below. With a typical home near $141,200, a few years of missed bills plus penalties can take a visible bite out of a sale price.

sections.h2: Do Hancock County rental owners owe an occupational fee?
sections.html:
Yes. The county's occupational tax page says every person or business with activity in Hancock County pays on net profits, and it names rental property owners, farmers and home based businesses in that group. The rate on business profits has been 1.60 percent since January 1, 2020, and an annual business license costs $10.

Employees working inside the county pay 1.60 percent of gross wages, withheld by the employer. Two exceptions apply: a company employing more than 100 people in manufacturing in the county does not owe the net profits fee, and neither does a business that pays the county a franchise tax.

A landlord selling a Hancock County rental should expect a net profits return for the year of the sale. The Occupational Tax Office, upstairs on the third floor, answers at 270-927-8788.

sections.h2: How can I contest a Hancock County assessment?
sections.html:
Meet the PVA first. Call 270-927-6846 to book a conference in the spring inspection window, which no appeal can skip. If the talk ends without a deal, you have one workday after the window closes to file with the clerk upstairs, along with the value you claim.

The local appeals board, three people, hears the case about five weeks later and expects evidence from you. The Kentucky Board of Tax Appeals hears anything further. Ask the PVA which sales it relied on, then bring your own comparable sales.

sections.h2: Who gets the homestead exemption in Hancock County?
sections.html: Owners aged 65 and up, and owners classified as totally disabled, can ask the PVA to lower the taxable value of their own residence. KRS 132.810 allows one exemption per household unit and treats a manufactured house as a unit. After a sale, the old owner reports the transfer and the new owner applies separately. Ask the PVA for the dollar figure in force.

sections.h2: What should a Hancock County seller check before closing?
sections.html:
A short checklist keeps surprises away from the table.

  • Confirm the deed carries a mailing address for the new owner's tax bill, which KRS 382.135 requires.
  • Ask the sheriff whether a current year bill is open and who will pay it, since the bill covers a full calendar year.
  • Search the parcel through the clerk's website, which links a delinquent tax tool (DTax) and eCCLIX, a viewer for filed land records that helps when a house came through an estate.
  • Pull permits for any addition. Planning and Zoning is at 200 Court Square, P.O. Box 692, open Monday, Wednesday and Friday from 8 a.m. to noon at 270-927-8169.

The Hancock County Urban Planning Commission holds evening meetings every other month, starting the first Monday of February.

sections.h2: What happens to an unpaid Hancock County bill?
sections.html:
A bill still open when April 15 ends leaves the sheriff and lands with the clerk as a certificate of delinquency. The clerk's DTax tool shows what the county believes is owed on a parcel, with a warning that the clerk fixes the true figure at payment or sale. Interest, a clerk commission and later an attorney commission pile on, and a buyer of the certificate adds more. A seller who plans to list in summer should pay or collect a written payoff before certificate sales begin in July.

Back taxes do not block a sale. The settlement agent pays the payoff from the proceeds, the same way it works with a cash buyer who purchases as is.

faqs.q: Do rental owners in Hancock County pay occupational tax?
faqs.a: Yes. Rental property owners pay on net profits at 1.60 percent, plus a $10 annual business license. The Occupational Tax Office at 270-927-8788 takes the forms.

faqs.q: When does the Hancock County Urban Planning Commission meet?
faqs.a: Every other month, starting with the first Monday of February. Meetings begin at 7 p.m. on the third floor of the Administration Building, 225 Main Cross Street.

faqs.q: How can I view recorded deeds for a Hancock County house?
faqs.a: Through eCCLIX on the County Clerk's website, which lets you view or print filed documents. Questions go to 270-927-6117.

faqs.q: I bought a Hancock County home and never got a tax bill. Who do I call?
faqs.a: The sheriff at 270-927-6247 can provide a copy. The PVA mails the bill to the address in the deed until preparation begins in mid September, which is why that address matters.

faqs.q: Is the PVA or the sheriff the office that takes the payment?
faqs.a: The sheriff. The PVA's role ends at valuation, and payments go to the Hancock County Sheriff's Office downstairs on the first floor.
